newsitem.title: NICARAGUA: Sandinista strike starts peacefully in Nicaragua.
newsitem.headline: Sandinista strike starts peacefully in Nicaragua.

text.p: Sandinista unions and grassroots groups began a national strike on Monday to protest the Nicaraguan government's economic policy, but no violence was reported, police said.
"At this moment, the situation is totally under control ... there have been no acts of violence," Police Chief Franco Montealegre told reporters.

In the past some major Sandinista-led street protests have led to bloody shootouts between protesters and police. The Sandinista Front, which came to power in a 1979 revolution, is now the country's main opposition party.

Fears of a violent protest were raised on Monday when local newspaper La Tribuna published an interview with former President Daniel Ortega in which he warned the Sandinistas would be obliged to "take up arms" if the government did not cede to the strikers' demands of easing an austerity plan.

"If we let the government continue applying its dictatorial project there will be no alternative but to take up arms once again to end the dictatorship," Ortega, a former guerrilla commander who was president from 1984 to 1990, said.

Local radio reports said protesters blocked highways around Nicaragua and set up barricades on some streets in Managua, the capital. Some bus and taxi unions were on strike, but buses and taxis were seen working. Stores and businesses opened normally but workers reported problems getting to work.
Strike leaders said a mass protest march to Managua's National Assembly was planned.
Montealegre said police had deployed 5,500 police officers and 500 anti-riot police across the country and had met no resistance in taking down the barricades.
Late Sunday, President Arnoldo Aleman made a special live broadcast to the nation calling for calm on Monday and inviting Ortega to meet with him to negotiate a peaceful solution to the crisis.
